name: Aromatherapy

lead: Aromatherapy is the practice of using aromatic plant oils, most often lavender, tea tree, peppermint, rosemary, citrus and frankincense, to promote relaxation and well-being. People usually inhale the scent from a diffuser or apply a diluted oil during a massage or in the bath.

In appearance terms, its appeal runs through chains such as calmer mood, better sleep and lower stress, which people associate with a rested face, plus the simple pleasure of scent as part of grooming. Systematic reviews of aromatherapy have reported improvements in self-rated sleep quality and anxiety, although the studies vary widely in design.

paras: Practitioners typically use a diffuser, a few drops on a pillow or tissue, an aroma massage with a carrier oil, or a scented bath, often in the evening to wind down. Some products combine essential oils with skincare or haircare, such as tea tree in blemish-focused products. Trials of sleep and anxiety have usually run for a few weeks, with sessions of 20 minutes or more.

Undiluted oils can irritate skin and cause allergic sensitisation, and some citrus oils can cause phototoxic reactions in sunlight. Ingesting essential oils can cause poisoning, and some oils are toxic to pets. Lavender and tea tree oils have been linked in case reports to breast tissue growth in prepubertal boys. There are no US quality standards for essential oils, and the phrase "therapeutic grade" has no regulatory meaning.

angle.text: People use aromatherapy as a wind-down routine, as an aroma massage, or through scented skincare and bath products. The appearance benefit they describe is a rested, relaxed look and a pleasant personal scent, reached through sleep and stress rather than any direct change to the face.

lead: Aromatherapy is the use of aromatic plant materials, chiefly essential oils, to support psychological and physical well-being. The oils are inhaled, applied diluted to the skin in massage, or added to bath water, and the practice is generally positioned as a complementary therapy rather than a replacement for medical care.[1][2]

For people interested in how they look, aromatherapy sits at the end of an indirect chain: relaxation and calmer mood, better sleep and lower stress, and a fresher, more rested appearance. It also overlaps with grooming, since scent is part of personal presentation and oils such as tea tree and lavender appear in skincare, haircare and bath products.[1]

Research on aromatherapy is mostly clinical and symptom-focused. A 2021 meta-analysis of 30 studies on adults and older adults reported a statistically significant combined effect on sleep quality, and a 2020 meta-analysis examined anxiety.[3][4] Reviews also describe its use for pain, nausea, preoperative anxiety and stress in hospital settings, alongside safety cautions about skin reactions and toxicity.[5][6]
infobox: Lavender, tea tree, peppermint, eucalyptus, citrus, frankincense
No US standard for oil quality; products regulated as cosmetics or by claims [1]

paras: Aromatherapy uses concentrated volatile extracts from flowers, leaves, fruit peel, resin and other plant parts. The most common methods are inhaling the scent from a diffuser, pillow or inhaler, applying diluted oil to the skin during massage, and adding oil to a bath. Oils are normally diluted in a carrier oil before touching skin.[1]

Commonly used oils and their traditional associations include lavender for relaxation and sleep, tea tree for skin blemishes and antimicrobial use, peppermint for headaches and alertness, rosemary for focus, citrus oils for uplift, and frankincense for mood and inflammation.[2] Proponents describe a principle of synergy among the many compounds in an oil, and a pathway in which scent reaches the brain's limbic system, which is involved in emotion and stress responses.[2]

Essential oils and their supposed healing properties are described in antiquity, including in the first-century De Materia Medica by Dioscorides, and distillation of oils such as rose was refined by Ibn Sina in the eleventh century.[1] The word "aromatherapy" first appeared in print in 1937 in the book Aromathérapie by French chemist René-Maurice Gattefossé, and the French surgeon Jean Valnet later promoted essential oils as antiseptics for wounded soldiers during World War II.[1]

Aromatherapy is not a cosmetic procedure, so its connection to looks is through routine and well-being. People use evening diffusing and aroma massage as part of a sleep and stress routine, and describe a more rested face as the result. Essential oils also feature in scented skincare, bath, body and haircare products, where cosmetic products are subject to the usual safety requirements.[1]
Tea tree oil in particular is described in review literature as having antimicrobial properties used for acne and minor skin concerns.[2]

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of 30 studies of aromatherapy and sleep quality in adults and older adults reported a combined effect size of 0.74 for sleep quality, with larger effects in aroma massage studies, East Asian studies and quasi-experimental designs.[3] A 2024 meta-analysis focused on older adults, and a 2023 review of non-drug interventions in intensive care looked at sleep and delirium.[7][8]

A 2020 meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials examined aromatherapy and anxiety.[4] Randomized trials have tested lavender oil for pain and anxiety after caesarean section, lavender and chamomile inhalation for depression, anxiety and stress in older people living at home, and aromatherapy combined with music around breast cancer surgery.[9][10][11] A 2024 comprehensive review describes applications and safety considerations across clinical aromatherapy.[5]

Wider reviews note that the evidence base is mixed and that many studies are small. Cochrane reviews covering nausea after surgery, labour pain, dementia-related behaviours and cancer symptoms reported mixed results, and a 2015 Australian government review found no clear evidence of effectiveness for health conditions.[1] No published trial has studied aromatherapy as a way to change facial appearance.

A nursing review notes that essential oils can be flammable, cause dermatitis, be phototoxic and cause chemical burns, and cause toxicity or death if taken by mouth.[6] Citrus oils are among those linked to phototoxic reactions, and wintergreen oil may increase bleeding risk in people taking warfarin.[1] Lavender and tea tree oils have been linked to breast tissue growth in prepubertal boys in case reports and may act as endocrine disruptors.[1] In 2021 an aromatherapy spray was recalled in the United States after bacterial contamination was linked to four cases of melioidosis and two deaths.[1]

In the US, aromatherapy fragrances are not approved as prescription drugs; products marketed for therapeutic use fall under FDA oversight, cosmetics must meet safety requirements, and advertising claims are regulated by the FTC. There are no US standards for essential oil quality.[1]
